job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Sam Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly it's slow. I get up around nine, check the job boards on my laptop at the kitchen table, send two or three applications, and then my mum Rosa gets back from her night shift at the hospital and we have breakfast. Two evenings a week I stack shelves at a supermarket on the ring road to cover my phone and loan payments.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What was the last stretch of study like, and what are you hoping for next?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did computer science at a university in the Midlands and scraped a pass. My final project was a bus timetable app in Java for the local route, and it worked, but I had no internship because I was working weekends. I want a steady junior developer job at a company that treats people decently, and so far I've sent about 70 applications and had two replies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I expected, honestly. The hype was always louder than the product. At work I'd say the shelves still need stacking, and online I'd say companies should stop blaming robots for not hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my problem is the same as now. There are fewer junior jobs than graduates, and a plateau doesn't fix that. I still have debt from the loan and a mum who's tired, and I'm not any closer to a proper job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, maybe 15 a week, and ask my old lecturer to look over my CV again. I'd keep the shelf-stacking shifts and try to add a third evening, which is about 90 pounds more a month. I'd also join the graduate branch of a tech workers' union if there is one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, mostly. It's not a crisis, but every week without an offer feels like I'm falling behind people who got internships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the plateau doesn't fix the job shortage. Who do you think is responsible for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Employers, mainly. They want three years of experience for a junior role and they won't train anyone. Government lets them get away with it, because there's no pressure to hire people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if the months drag on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My phone contract and the money I give towards my sister Dani's school trips. Mum would never ask, but I know she's counting what I put in at the end of the month. I'd rather cut my own stuff than let her feel that.

say: AI was always more hype than product, so my **problem** is the same as before.
Employers want three years of experience for junior roles and won't train anyone.
think: A plateau doesn't fix the **shortage** of junior jobs, and I'm not closer to a real job.
I still carry student **debt**, and my mum is tired.
do: Send about **15 applications** a week and get my old lecturer to check my CV.
Add a third evening of shelf stacking, roughly **90 pounds** more a month.
Look for a graduate branch of a tech workers' **union**.
feel: Tense but not in crisis; every week without an **offer** feels like falling behind.
S0.quote: There are fewer junior jobs than graduates, and a plateau doesn't fix that.
fieldNote: Anger points at **employers** and government, not at the technology.
Already carrying **job-hunt** stress before AI comes into it.
Quietly protects his **mother's** budget by cutting his own spending first.

steps.text: Send 15 job applications a week to junior developer roles
Add a third evening shelf-stacking shift for about 90 pounds a month
Cut the phone contract before touching money for his sister
Ask about joining a tech workers' union graduate branch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly my worry. Writing, checking, coding, those are the things I trained for, and now software does them. Online I'd say there should be rules on how fast firms can swap people for programs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the junior jobs go first. A team of ten that used to hire two graduates now hires none, because one senior with a tool does the work. I'm the type who never touched those tools, which makes it worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to finally try them, which I hate. Maybe one evening a week on a free course, and I'd keep the shelf job. I'd also write to my local councillor about retraining money, and I'd go to a union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels unfair. I paid for a degree for a ladder, and the bottom rung is being sawn off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never touched the tools. Why is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like knowing how things work. If a tool writes the code for me, I don't learn anything and I don't trust it. But I can see that argument doesn't pay the bills, and that's what bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend in the same spot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to get a trade certificate alongside the degree, maybe in networks or electronics. Something where a person still has to turn up and plug the cable in.

say: Firms need **rules** on how fast they swap people for programs.
Writing, checking and coding are exactly what I trained for.
think: Teams of ten that hired two graduates now hire **none**, because one senior with a tool does the work.
I never touched the tools, which makes my position **worse**.
do: Try the tools at last, with one **evening** a week on a free course.
Keep the shelf job and write to my **councillor** about retraining money.
Go to a **union** meeting and look at a networking certificate.
feel: It feels **unfair**: I paid for a ladder and the bottom rung is being sawn off.
S1.quote: I paid for a degree for a ladder, and the bottom rung is being sawn off.
fieldNote: **Distrust** of AI tools comes from wanting to understand the code, but he admits it doesn't pay bills.
Sees **junior roles** as the first casualty and himself as unprepared.
Leans on **collective** and political routes rather than personal reinvention.

steps.text: Take one free AI coding course evening a week
Get a networking or electronics certificate alongside the degree
Write to the local councillor about retraining money
Attend a union meeting for tech workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready, and that's the scandal. Two years is no time for a government to write a single law. I'd tell people online to push for a basic income before it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm terrified. If AI does almost all thinking work in two years, my degree is worth nothing before I've used it once. I don't have a plan, and with three people's wages in this house I can't draw one up quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd probably freeze for a month. After that, I'd ask my mum's hospital about porter or healthcare assistant work, anything physical, since robots are three years behind. I'd stop paying extra on my loan and keep every pound in my account. And I'd march with whoever organises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like standing on a train platform watching the train arrive and not knowing which way to jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd freeze for a month. What does that month look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit at the kitchen table refreshing job boards that have nothing on them. Dani would ask me questions I can't answer and mum would go quiet. I'd be useless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum, and my uncle Ravi, who has a van business. He'd give me hand work, probably. I hate that I'd be asking, though.

say: Two years is no time for any government to write a single **law**.
People should push for a **basic income** before it lands.
think: My degree could be worth **nothing** before I've used it once.
With three wages in the house, I can't draw up a **plan** quickly.
do: Freeze for about a **month**, then ask my mum's hospital about healthcare assistant work.
Stop extra **loan** payments and keep every pound in my account.
Ask my uncle **Ravi** for van work and march with any group organising.
feel: **Sick**, like watching a train arrive and not knowing which way to jump.
S2.quote: I'm terrified. If AI does almost all thinking work in two years, my degree is worth nothing before I've used it once.
fieldNote: **No plan** and little confidence he could make one; the freeze is honest rather than dramatic.
Looks to **robots** lagging three years as a reason to seek physical work.
**Shame** about asking family for help sits next to real need.

steps.text: Apply for healthcare assistant jobs at his mother's hospital
Stop extra loan payments and hold every pound in savings
Ask Uncle Ravi for van delivery work
March with whichever group organises for basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, but it's long enough that people with power have no excuse. I'd say unions should bargain on this now, not after the layoffs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd probably be okay at the very start, then in trouble by 2031 if I haven't built anything. Five years is enough time to get a job and lose it again. That's the part that keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, get any developer job, even badly paid, so I have a name on my CV. Then use the next few years to move toward something with hands in it, like network cabling or electrical testing. I'd save about 150 a month, and I'd try one AI tool a week even though I don't want to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, but not hopeless. At least there's a window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you try one AI tool a week if you hate the idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A deadline and a reason. If a job asks me, I'll learn it, I'm not stupid. I just won't pay for the privilege of automating myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if a job never comes in that window?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my uncle Ravi's van business full time and try to turn my IT knowledge into a service for small shops. It's not what I dreamed of, but it's still work.

say: Five years is short, but powerful people have **no excuse**.
Unions should bargain over AI now, **before** the layoffs.
think: I might be fine at first and in trouble by **2031** if I haven't built anything.
Five years is enough time to get a job and **lose** it.
do: Take any developer job first, even badly paid, to get a name on my **CV**.
Save about **150 a month** and try one AI tool a week.
Move toward hands-on work such as **network cabling** or electrical testing.
feel: **Heavy** but not hopeless, because at least there's a window.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to get a job and lose it again. That's the part that keeps me awake.
fieldNote: The **window** gives him a plan, but he still expects to lose a first job.
**Resistance** to AI tools is practical: he will learn when a job demands it.
Fallback is the **family van** business, which he treats as acceptable but second best.

steps.text: Accept any junior developer job, even low paid, for the CV
Save 150 a month from shelf-stacking and any new wages
Learn one AI tool a week once a job requires it
Move toward network cabling or electrical testing work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years sounds like forever until you're 23 with no offer. I'd say we need real retraining schemes paid for by the firms that profit. I'd say it publicly and at the union branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, ten years feels survivable. I can get a job, pay off my loan, maybe start a family before the big change. But I worry I'll spend those ten years running to keep still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, take whatever I get, and go part time on a trade course in electronics once I have wages. I'd put 200 a month into savings, and I'd help Dani choose her degree more carefully than I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but still a knot. There's more room to breathe, and I still don't have the offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister Dani to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something where a person has to be in the room. Nursing like mum, or an electrician's apprenticeship. I wouldn't tell my sister Dani to do computing, and that hurts to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your worries doesn't go away with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The debt, and the fact that no one wants to train juniors. Ten years doesn't fix that, only pressure on employers does.

say: We need real **retraining** schemes paid for by the firms that profit.
I'd say it publicly and at the **union** branch.
think: Ten years feels survivable: get a job, pay the **loan**, maybe start a family.
I worry I'll spend the decade **running** to keep still.
do: Keep applying and take whatever **job** comes, then study electronics part time.
Put **200 a month** into savings once I have wages.
Help my sister Dani choose her **degree** more carefully than I did.
feel: **Calmer**, but still a knot, since the offer hasn't come.
S4.quote: I wouldn't tell my sister Dani to do computing, and that hurts to say.
fieldNote: Extra **time** lowers panic but not the structural worry about employers refusing to train juniors.
**Family-minded**: plans around his sister's choices and a future family.
Would **steer** a younger relative away from his own field, a telling admission.

steps.text: Take the first junior job offered and keep applying for better
Study electronics part time on an evening trade course
Put 200 a month into a savings account
Help his sister Dani pick a degree or apprenticeship

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028. I have no plan and no money to make one, and my mum's wage is what keeps this house going. What would help is a real income floor, retraining that pays you while you do it, and employers forced to take on juniors.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd just add that people like me aren't lazy or against technology. I'm against being thrown away for it. If firms and governments shared the gains, I'd be first in the queue to learn the new tools.

headlineQuote: People like me aren't lazy or against technology. I'm against being thrown away for it.
portrait: Sam is a 23-year-old **computer science** graduate with a pass, no internship and about 70 applications sent.
He lives with his mother Rosa, a night-shift nurse, and his sister Dani, and **stacks shelves** two evenings a week.
He leans left, blames **employers and government** for the junior job shortage, and has never used AI tools.
His mood climbs from anxious to **panicked** as the warning shrinks, because he has no plan and thin money.
His answer is collective: unions, **retraining** schemes and family help, plus hands-on work as a fallback.
biggestWorry: The **2028** AGI case, with no plan, no time and only his mother's wage holding the house up.
whatWouldHelp: An **income floor**, paid retraining and employers forced to hire juniors.
